hints: Notice the given acceleration-time graph starts at zero, rises to a maximum and then falls back to zero, staying positive throughout.
Recall that on a velocity-time graph the gradient equals $a$, and the change in velocity equals the area under the acceleration-time graph.
Ask what the velocity gradient must be at the start, at peak acceleration, and at the end when acceleration is zero again.
walkthrough: The object starts from rest, so the velocity-time graph must start at $v = 0$ at $t = 0$. The acceleration is always $a \ge 0$, so velocity can only increase or stay constant.
Use $a = \frac{\Delta v}{\Delta t}$. This means the gradient of the $v$-$t$ graph at any time equals the value of $a$ at that time, and total $\Delta v$ is the area under the $a$-$t$ graph.
At the start $a = 0$, so the $v$-$t$ graph starts flat with zero gradient. As $a$ grows, the $v$-$t$ gradient grows, so $v$ curves upward more steeply.
When $a$ is maximum, the $v$-$t$ graph is steepest. This is a point of inflection. As $a$ then decreases, the $v$-$t$ gradient decreases, so the curve flattens.
At the end $a$ returns to zero, so the $v$-$t$ gradient returns to zero. Velocity reaches a maximum constant value and does not decrease because $a$ was never negative.
Only graph A starts at zero, shows increasing gradient then decreasing gradient, and levels off horizontally. This is option A.

A.explanation: Velocity starts at zero, increases with a gradient that follows the acceleration hump, then levels off to a maximum when acceleration returns to zero.

B.explanation: This copies the shape of the acceleration hump, but velocity would have to fall back to zero which would need negative acceleration.

C.explanation: Velocity cannot become negative or oscillate because the given acceleration is never negative, so velocity must keep increasing.

D.explanation: This shows a continuously increasing gradient, which would need continuously increasing acceleration, not an acceleration that falls back to zero.
